otherDevice.text: You are reading the instructions for: {reading}. This device: {here}.

usb.android: The phone's browser can't use a cable to Arduino: connect via Bluetooth.
usb.ios: iPhone and iPad don't allow a cable to Arduino: you need a Bluetooth LE module.
usb.ok: You can connect Arduino with the USB cable.
usb.chromiumOff: Serial connection is disabled in this browser: update Chrome or Edge.
usb.otherBrowser: {browser} can't talk to Arduino: open this page in Chrome or Edge.

ble.off: Supported, but Bluetooth is off or missing: turn it on in the settings.
ble.ok: You can connect to a Bluetooth LE module (HM-10, AT-09, HC-08).
ble.ios: iPhone browsers don't give web pages access to Bluetooth: install Bluefy (free, App Store) and open MosaicusNeo there.
ble.chromiumOff: Web Bluetooth not available (on Linux, enable it in chrome://flags).
ble.otherBrowser: {browser} doesn't support Web Bluetooth: use Chrome or Edge.

hc06.ios: The HC-06 uses classic Bluetooth, which iPhone and iPad don't support: you need a BLE module.
hc06.androidOk: You can use the HC-06: pair it first in the Bluetooth settings (PIN 1234).
hc06.androidChrome: Requires Chrome 138 or later (here: {version}): update it from the Play Store.
hc06.androidOther: Requires Chrome for Android 138 or later.
hc06.pcWarn: Works only if the HC-06 is already paired in the system's Bluetooth settings. A BLE module doesn't need pairing.

secure.ok: Page served over https: USB and Bluetooth allowed.
secure.no: Open the app from its https address: without it, the browser blocks USB and Bluetooth.

installed.ok: It also opens without a network connection.
installed.other: Optional: browser menu → “Install MosaicusNeo”. Then it also opens without a network connection.

port.windows: In the top menu: Arduino Uno and the port COM3, COM4… that appears when you plug in the cable.
port.mac: In the top menu: Arduino Uno and the port /dev/cu.usbmodem… (clones: /dev/cu.wchusbserial…).
port.linux: In the top menu: Arduino Uno and /dev/ttyACM0 (or /dev/ttyUSB0). No permission: sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER, then log out and back in.

connectHow.pc: “Connect Arduino” and choose the USB port. With a BLE module: menu ▾ → “Bluetooth LE”.
connectHow.android: HC-06 already paired: “Connect via Bluetooth”. BLE module: menu ▾ → “Bluetooth LE”.

s1.d: Firefox and Safari can't talk to Arduino.

s4.t: Connect Arduino with the USB cable
s4.d: “Connect Arduino” → choose the port{port} → wait for “Arduino ready”.

s5.d: “Start”, “Stop”, select a range on the chart and “Analyze the range”. See <measure>Measuring</measure>.

s1.t: From a computer: upload the firmware
s1.d: The phone can't program Arduino. Just once: <firmware>Uploading the firmware</firmware>.

s2.d: HC-06 or BLE (HM-10, AT-09, HC-08): it's a component like any other, in “Add a component” → Bluetooth (or from the ▾ menu of “Connect”). The diagram includes it.

s3.t: From the computer: configure the module
s3.d: Just once, with Arduino on USB: <field>Measuring wirelessly</field>.

s4.t: On the phone, in Chrome: connect
s4.d: HC-06: pair “MosaicusNeo” in the Bluetooth settings (PIN 1234), then “Connect via Bluetooth”. BLE: menu ▾ → “Bluetooth LE”.

s5.t: Power Arduino from a power bank and measure
s5.d: The screen stays on during the measurement. The Notebook saves every 30 s.

ios.note: On iPhone and iPad you need a Bluetooth LE module (HM-10, AT-09/BT05, HC-08) and the free Bluefy browser. The cable and the HC-06 don't work: it's an iOS limitation.

s1.t: From a computer: upload the firmware

s2.d: Add the Bluetooth LE component (in “Add a component” → Bluetooth): the diagram includes it.

s3.t: From the computer: configure the module
s3.d: Just once, with Arduino on USB: <field>Measuring wirelessly</field>.

s4.d: From the App Store. Type the app's address in Bluefy's address bar.

s5.d: Arduino on the power bank, then “Connect via Bluetooth LE” → “MosaicusNeo”.

s1.d: Large text and lighter charts for slow whiteboards. <lim>Turn it on now</lim> (also from the Appearance menu, at the top).

s2.t: Choose where the data comes from
s2.d: The whiteboard can't use a cable to Arduino. You can: use a Bluetooth module (as on Android, with Chrome); measure from the classroom computer and project it; sign in with the same account and open measurements made elsewhere from the Notebook.

s3.d: Firmware and module setup are done once from a computer: <field>Measuring wirelessly</field>.

s4.t: To discuss the data in class
s4.d: Notebook → “Analyze”: in Analysis, fits and tangents also work by touch.

share.open: On the other device, open this address: {url}

startDevice.unknown: I can't recognize this device: the steps below are for a computer.
startDevice.cannot: This device can't connect to Arduino yet. Open “What works on this device” below to see what's missing and how to fix it.
startDevice.otherHint: Reading here but measuring with another device? Choose it from “Instructions for”, at the top.

start.intro: MosaicusNeo reads the sensors connected to Arduino, shows real-time charts, saves the measurements and analyzes them. It runs in the browser, even offline.

need.arduino: Arduino Uno or a clone (e.g. Elegoo UNO R3), with its USB cable.
need.parts: The components for the experiment, a breadboard and jumper wires.
need.computer: A computer with Chrome or Edge: needed to upload the firmware and to measure over the cable.
need.optional: Optional: a Bluetooth module and a power bank, to measure wirelessly with the phone.

start.simulator: No hardware? Press Simulator: it generates realistic data for every experiment.

firmware.intro: The firmware is the program that runs on Arduino. There is just one for all experiments: you upload it once, then the app tells it which components to read.
firmware.pcOnly: The firmware is uploaded from a computer (Windows, Mac, Linux or Chromebook) with the USB cable: the device you chose ({device}) can't program Arduino. Then you measure with the {target, select, board {whiteboard} other {phone}} via Bluetooth. The steps below are for {os}: to change it, choose your computer from “Instructions for”, at the top.

ide.windows: Download it from arduino.cc/en/software: choose Windows (the installer, or the Microsoft Store version) and install it. On a school PC without admin rights, ask the technician.
ide.mac: Download it from arduino.cc/en/software: choose macOS (Apple Silicon for Macs with an M chip, Intel for older ones), open the .dmg and drag Arduino IDE into Applications.
ide.linux: Download the AppImage from arduino.cc/en/software, make it executable (right-click → Properties → Allow executing, or chmod +x) and open it.

s1.d: Chromebooks can't install Arduino IDE: in Chrome, go to <cloud>app.arduino.cc</cloud> and sign in with a free Arduino account. If it asks to install a plugin or app, follow its instructions.

s2.t: Create a sketch with the firmware
s2.d: Create a new sketch and replace all its code with the contents of mosaicusneo_firmware.ino (open the downloaded file, or copy it from “Code on GitHub”).

s4.d: From the menu at the top of the editor: Arduino Uno, on the port that appears when you plug in the cable.

s5.d: The TX/RX LEDs blink; after a few seconds the editor says the upload is done.

s2.d: Open mosaicusneo_firmware.ino. If the IDE asks to move it into a folder with the same name, confirm with OK.

s3.t: Connect Arduino with the USB cable
s3.d: The “ON” LED lights up. If there is a Bluetooth module on D0, unplug its TXD wire now.

s5.d: The TX/RX LEDs blink; after a few seconds Done uploading appears.

s6.d: Close the Arduino IDE or editor, press Connect Arduino and choose the port. The status becomes Arduino ready · firmware {v}.

ch340.windows: Clone with a CH340 chip and no COM port? Install the CH340 driver for Windows and plug the cable back in.
ch340.mac: Clone with a CH340 chip and no port? Recent versions of macOS include the driver; on older ones, install the CH340 driver for macOS and plug the cable back in.

firmware.noAdmin: Can't install programs (e.g. on a school PC)? The <cloud>Arduino Cloud Editor</cloud> runs in the browser, but it needs a small helper program, the Arduino Cloud Agent: ask the technician to install one of the two.
firmware.serialBusy: The serial port can be opened by only one program at a time: with the IDE's Serial Monitor open, MosaicusNeo can't connect, and vice versa.

wiring.intro: Every lab has its own wiring diagram, made from its components and the pins you chose: open the lab and go to the “Wiring” tab. There you'll find the breadboard diagram (or the pin map), the parts list and the steps, hole by hole.
wiring.bb1: The five holes of a column (a–e or f–j) are connected to each other; the central groove separates them.
wiring.bb2: The side rails run the whole length: red (+) for 5V, blue (−) for GND.
wiring.bb3: D0 and D1 are reserved for the USB cable and Bluetooth: don't connect components to them.
wiring.where: The diagram updates as you add or change components. Bluetooth, SD card and button are components like any other: add them to the lab and they appear in the diagram.
wiring.empty: The open lab has no Arduino components yet: add some in the “Components” tab first.

s1.d: From the list on the left. The components and their pins appear at the top.

s2.d: “Wiring” tab (on the right; at the bottom on a phone).

s4.d: Above the “Start” button, e.g. “Group 3 · inclined plane”. If you leave it empty: the experiment's title with date and time.

s5.d: With “Start” the points arrive in real time. With “Stop” the measurement is saved in the Notebook.

s6.d: Drag on the chart: the range is highlighted on all charts. Double-click to clear; pinch or Ctrl + scroll wheel to zoom.

s7.d: “Analyze the range” opens Analysis on the new panel. The “+” next to it adds the panel without changing page.

measure.m1: Charts: the menu above the charts chooses the quantities. The “raw data” are the readings before conversion.
measure.m2: Table and Export (icons on the right): the numeric values, or Excel, CSV, image, GPX files.
measure.m3: Zero (crosshair, with the ultrasonic sensor): the current position becomes zero.
measure.m4: Notebook: all measurements, with search and filters. “Open” brings one back to Measure, “Analyze” sends it whole to Analysis.
measure.m5: Whiteboard mode (Appearance menu): large text and lighter charts, for whiteboards and slow PCs.

rigs.intro: Every lab, ready-made or your own, has a list of components: sensors, displays, LEDs and buzzers, each with its own pins and reading rate. Up to 6 sensors at once, even of the same type (e.g. two thermistors to compare two cups).
rigs.projectsIntro: Your own lab is a set of components you choose. You'll find it in “My labs”, at the top of the sidebar:
rigs.p2: Copy to My labs (in an experiment, “Components” tab): start from its components.
rigs.p3: With an account, your labs are available on all your devices.
rigs.personal: If you modify a ready-made experiment you get a personal version; “Restore” goes back to the original.

s1.d: On the right; on a phone, the button under the title.

s2.d: “Add a component” opens the catalog: search by name or quantity, filter by category.

s3.d: Pins already in use can't be selected. Analog sensors go on A0…A5.

s4.d: “One reading every … ms”. Limits: DHT at least 1000 ms, GPS one reading per second, sonar down to 30 ms.

s5.d: Calibration, positive direction, DHT model… The less used ones are in “Advanced options”.

rigs.phoneText: Without Arduino you can use the phone's accelerometer, gyroscope and microphone: experiments in the “Tools” section of the list, or the “Phone, no Arduino” category in “Add a component”. Open the app on the phone (Chrome on Android, Safari on iPhone) and press Enable sensors; on iPhone, confirm the permission. They can't be mixed with Arduino components in the same lab.
rigs.errorNote: With an error in the components (duplicate pin, too many sensors…) “Start” stays disabled; the message tells you how to fix it.

analysis.intro: Every range sent from Measure or from the Notebook becomes a panel, with chart, tools and data. Above the chart choose the quantities on the axes, including one as a function of another (e.g. T as a function of altitude).

range.d: Drag to choose the data. Range statistics: mean ± standard error of the mean (s/√n), standard deviation s, minimum and maximum, change Δy and average ratio Δy/Δx (e.g. average velocity).

eyeLine.d: Move the two handles until the line passes between the points (⬆⬇ count the points above and below), then tap two points on the line to read Δy/Δx. “Compare with least squares” compares it with the least-squares line.

tangent.d: Tap a point on the curve: slope at that point, e.g. the instantaneous velocity.

fit.d: Choose a model (line, parabola, exponential, damped sinusoid…): parameters with uncertainty and physical meaning. “Check residuals” shows the residuals. “Compare all models”: a table with s, R² and an assessment of the residuals; the best one is highlighted.

ruler.d: On a wave: place the two lines on two crests and enter how many periods N lie between them. T = Δt/N, f = 1/T.

sheet.d: All the values. “New column” computes a quantity from a formula (e.g. x^2, ln(T − 21), sqrt(L/g)).

analysis.r1: Save adds a result to the panel. The eye icon shows or hides it on the chart.
analysis.r2: A panel can be collapsed or duplicated, to try another analysis on the same data.
analysis.r3: Tick the panels and press Export to Excel: a summary sheet, one with all the results and one per panel.

wireless.intro: Two ways to measure without a cable to the computer. They are components like any other: add them from “Add a component”, or from the ▾ menu of “Connect”, and the diagram and the steps include them.

bt.d: Live charts on a phone or computer nearby, with Arduino on a power bank.

sd.d: Arduino records on its own, even for hours. You import the data afterwards.

wireless.sdTitle: SD card: Arduino on its own
wireless.buttonText: A button between a digital pin and GND (no resistor needed) starts and stops. With the SD card it starts and stops the recording. With the app connected, via cable or Bluetooth, it works like “Start” and “Stop”: handy when your hands are busy with the experiment. If you connect the app while Arduino is recording to the card, the recording is closed and you measure as usual. With a buzzer, Arduino stays quiet while waiting and ticks softly every 5 s while recording, so you can tell from a distance that it's working.

sd.intro: With a microSD card Arduino measures on its own, powered by a power bank or a battery: no computer, no phone, even for hours. Add the SD card component (Storage group), or pick Record to SD card from the ▾ menu of “Connect”.
sd.n1: A microSD module with a regulator (“Micro SD Card Adapter”): it runs on 5V. It always uses D10 (CS), D11 (MOSI), D12 (MISO) and D13 (SCK): move components that used them to other pins.
sd.n2: A microSD card formatted as FAT32, up to 32 GB (larger ones come as exFAT: reformat them to FAT32).
sd.n3: Optional: a button between a digital pin and GND (no resistor).

s1.d: With Arduino connected via the USB cable: in the SD card component's card press Prepare Arduino. Arduino receives sensors, pins and rates, saves them (they persist when powered off) and tests the card.

s2.d: Unplug the cable and connect a power bank to the USB socket, or a 9 V battery to the barrel jack.

s3.d: With the button: press to start, press again to stop; each recording is a new file (LOG00001.NEO, LOG00002.NEO…). Without a button: it records from when you switch it on until you switch it off. Arduino saves every 2 s: cutting the power loses at most the last few moments.

s4.d: Put the card in the computer and press Import from SD card (in the Notebook or in the component's card): each file becomes a measurement, with the usual quantities, charts and Analysis.

sd.statusNote: The display, LED and buzzer tell you what's happening: “SD CARD · PRESS” waits for the button, “● SD REC · 1:23” is recording, “ERROR · SD” if the card is missing or not FAT32.

field.iosNote: On iPhone and iPad: BLE modules only, and only in the Bluefy browser.
field.intro: With a Bluetooth module and a power bank you measure outdoors, with the phone. Add Bluetooth HC-06 or Bluetooth LE to the lab (or pick it from the ▾ menu of “Connect”: it joins the components automatically). Both types connect to the same pins, D0 and D1 (see Wiring the components).

table.nothing: nothing: you pick it from the app

c1.t: Wire the module as in the diagram
c1.d: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TXD → D0, RXD ← D1 through the 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ voltage divider.

c2.t: Connect Arduino to the computer with the USB cable
c2.d: The module's LED blinks: no phone is connected.

c4.d: In “Wiring”, with Bluetooth on, in the Bluetooth module's step.

c5.d: The module is now called “MosaicusNeo” and communicates at 115200 baud, like Arduino.

p1.t: Power Arduino from a power bank
p1.d: The USB cable goes to the power bank, not to the computer.

p2.d: Android: Chrome. iPhone and iPad: Bluefy (free, App Store), with the app's address.

p3.d: HC-06: pair “MosaicusNeo” in the Bluetooth settings (PIN 1234), then “Connect via Bluetooth”. BLE: menu ▾ → Bluetooth LE → “MosaicusNeo” (on iPhone: “Connect via Bluetooth LE”).

p4.d: The screen stays on during the measurement and the Notebook saves every 30 s: if the phone locks up, the data are kept.

field.gpsText: The first fix takes from 30 seconds to a few minutes, outdoors with a clear sky; the module's LED blinks when it has a position. Points without a position stay in the table but don't appear on the map. The map colors the points by the chosen quantity. Export to GPX (Google Earth, Strava) or GeoJSON (QGIS).

outputs.intro: Display, RGB LED and buzzer show Arduino's status without looking at the phone. They are added like the other components: “Components” tab → Add a component, “Status display” category. They require firmware v{v} or later.

waiting.situation: Powered on, the app isn't connected
waiting.display: NO APP · WAIT · USB v2.0 (with a Bluetooth module: USB/BT 2.0)
waiting.beep: 1 beep every 3 s (silent with a Start/Stop button)

connected.display: LINK USB · READY · tap Start (over Bluetooth: “LINK BT”)
connected.beep: 1 beep every 3 s (silent with a Start/Stop button)

measuring.beep: silent (a “beep-beep” when it gets there); with a Start/Stop button, a short low tick every 5 s

outputs.buzzerNote: As long as the buzzer beeps, something isn't ready. When it's silent, Arduino is measuring normally.
outputs.buttonBeep: With a Start/Stop button it's different, because Arduino stays on for a long time and records only now and then: while waiting it's silent, and while recording it gives a short tick every 5 s, lower and slower than the problem beeps (on a passive buzzer it's also a lower note). The problem beeps stay the same.
outputs.gpsText: Right after power-on, or indoors, the GPS searches for satellites: yellow, 2 beeps, and the display shows the number of satellites in view. Outdoors the fix arrives within 30 seconds to a few minutes. If no data at all arrive from the GPS, check the wires: red, 3 beeps, “GPS wires?”.
outputs.mu1: If several sensors have a problem, the display shows them in turn every 2.5 seconds, errors first and then those still searching: “ERROR 1/2”, “ERROR 2/2”. LED and buzzer always follow the most serious.
outputs.mu2: With two sensors of the same type, the display tells which one by number: “#2” is the second DHT in the component list.
outputs.mu3: If Arduino rejects a component (duplicate pin, non-analog pin, second GPS), the display shows “BAD SETUP” with the reason until you fix the pins and restart the measurement.
outputs.mu4: While waiting for the app, the display shows how to connect and the firmware version: “USB v2.0”. Bluetooth is optional: after “Configure” in the Bluetooth step, if the module responds, Arduino remembers it and the display shows “USB/BT 2.0”.
outputs.d1: Arduino remembers the indicators: on later power-ups it immediately shows “waiting for the app”, even before you connect the phone.
outputs.d2: During the measurement the display shows the first quantity in large digits and the second below it, updated every second.
outputs.d3: “Test display, LED and buzzer” (“Components” tab, with Arduino connected) changes the LED's color, sounds the buzzer and writes “HELLO” on the display.
outputs.d4: The measurement card shows in small print what the display, LED and buzzer are showing at that moment.
outputs.d5: To silence the buzzer: option “Beep until everything is ready” → no (this also turns off the recording tick).
outputs.d6: Display, MPU-6050 accelerometer and MLX90614 infrared thermometer can share the two I2C pins (usually A4 and A5).

data.where: Notebook measurements and Analysis panels stay in this device's browser, even offline. Clearing browsing data deletes them: export what you want to keep.
data.account: With “Sign in” you create an account with email and password. Measurements, panels, your labs and preferences are saved to the cloud and are available on all your devices; measurements made before signing in also move to the account. When you sign out, the data disappear from the device but stay in the cloud: suitable for school computers.
data.delete: To delete the account: account menu → Delete account. The account and the data in the cloud are deleted immediately and permanently; export what you want to keep first.
data.f1: Excel (.xlsx): the data and a sheet with the components, pins and options used.
data.f2: CSV for Italian Excel (decimal comma) or standard CSV (Google Sheets, Python).
data.f3: Image of the charts; GPX and GeoJSON for GPS tracks.
data.f4: Raw data (CSV or Excel): the readings as they arrive from Arduino (ADC counts, echo µs, DHT bytes, NMEA fields), one row per reading. For scripts in Python, R or MATLAB.

noPort.a: Unsupported browser, charge-only cable, missing driver or port in use. Use Chrome or Edge on a computer; try another cable or another USB port; with a CH340 clone install the CH340 driver; close the Arduino IDE.

noFirmware.a: The MosaicusNeo firmware isn't on Arduino. Upload it: <firmware>Uploading the firmware</firmware>. With a Bluetooth module on D0, unplug the TXD wire during the upload.

oldFirmware.a: Recent features (your own labs, Bluetooth LE) require v{v}. Download the firmware again and re-upload it.

dht.q: The DHT11 gives empty values or “—”
dht.a: Wrong wiring or readings too frequent. Check DATA on the chosen pin and VCC to 5V; the bare sensor (4 pins) needs 10 kΩ between DATA and 5V. Read at most once per second (DHT22: every 2 s).

sonar.q: The sonar jumps or misses points
sonar.a: The echo gets lost or bounces off other objects. Use a large, flat target, between 5 cm and 3 m, with a clear beam. In the advanced options you can discard anomalous jumps and adjust the smoothing of velocity and acceleration.

thermistor.q: The thermistor temperature is off by a few degrees
thermistor.a: The configuration differs from the actual circuit. Check the “thermistor position in the divider” (between 5V and the pin, or between the pin and GND) and, in the advanced options, the thermistor's R₀ and B. A calibration offset is added to all values.

gps.q: The GPS can't find its position
gps.a: With “searching for satellites” the GPS is working but has no signal yet: move outdoors, away from tall buildings, and wait a few minutes. If no data arrive at all, check that the GPS TX is on the chosen “Arduino RX” pin.

bluetooth.q: The Bluetooth module doesn't show up
bluetooth.a1: HC-06: it isn't paired or the device doesn't support it. Pair it in the phone's settings (PIN 1234 or 0000); it works only on Android.
bluetooth.a2: BLE: you search for it from the app, not from the settings. If “MosaicusNeo” isn't there, the module isn't configured: look for HMSoft, BT05 or HC-08. On iPhone use Bluefy, not Safari.
bluetooth.a3: It connects but no data arrive: the module is still at 9600 baud. Repeat “Configure” with the USB cable (<field>Measuring wirelessly</field>).

slow.a: Underpowered device or too many charts. Turn on whiteboard mode (Appearance menu): it disables animations and draws lighter charts. Close other tabs; in long measurements show fewer charts (“Charts” menu).

problems.report: Problem not listed here? <issues>Report it on GitHub</issues>: describe the device, browser, components and what happens.
